A1.justification: Both PDFs concern the same Densest k-Subgraph relaxation with diagonal loading and retain identifiable shared theorems. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison despite substantial changes in emphasis and organization.

before.justification: V3 Section 4 reports original parameter-selection experiments and density/runtime comparisons on six real-world graphs in Figures 2–5.

after.justification: V4 Section 5 reports original convergence experiments on Facebook and a synthetic regular graph, with outcomes in Figures 2–3.

M1.justification: The quadratic relaxation is retained up to equivalent scaling, but v4 replaces ordinary Frank–Wolfe with SE-FW, adding deterministic two-coordinate saddle-escape steps and an adaptive triggering strategy. It also removes v3's separate sigmoid parameterization method optimized with AdamW.

E1.justification: Facebook is retained, but evaluations on web-Stanford, com-Youtube, soc-Pokec, as-Skitter, and com-Orkut are removed. V4 adds a random 10-regular graph with 100 vertices specifically to test a stationary initialization. This substantially narrows real-world coverage while adding a distinct synthetic failure scenario.

E2.justification: V3's reported comparisons with Greedy, rank-1 LRBO, L-ADMM, EXPP, and the density upper bound disappear. V4's Facebook comparison retains the two existing step-size rules: Bertsekas and Lacoste-Julien correspond to v3's Options I and II, respectively.

E3.justification: V4 replaces density/runtime evaluation across subgraph sizes with convergence diagnostics at k=20 and λ=1.5, versus v3's default λ=1. Frank–Wolfe gap and loaded objective value are added as evaluation metrics. The quantity ||x||²/k is retained, renamed from solution sparsity to integrality; uniform initialization is also retained.

E4.justification: V3's Facebook sensitivity analysis over λ=0, 0.1, 1, 10, and 100 is removed. Its step-size study at k=20 and 50 is reworked into an exact-convergence diagnostic at k=20. V4 additionally tests whether saddle escape overcomes a zero-gap uniform initialization on a regular graph.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new random-graph experiment introduces no uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: V3's multi-network density/runtime results and loading-sweep outcomes are removed. V4 reports new convergence trajectories at λ=1.5: Facebook reaches zero Frank–Wolfe gap and integrality one, while the synthetic graph exhibits saddle escape and convergence after about 14 iterations. These are results under changed methods/settings, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: V3's general tightness and local-maximizer monotonicity results survive as v4 Theorems 2.3 and 3.2. V4 adds stationarity/local-optimality characterizations, strict-saddle classification, attraction-basin bounds, quantitative escape bounds, and finite-step convergence analysis with proofs in Appendices D–L. V3's standalone extended Motzkin–Straus theorem and proof are removed, while their non-tightness implication is retained through attribution.

C1.justification: V3 emphasizes two projection-free methods and competitive density, runtime, and scalability. V4 centers its abstract, contributions, and conclusion on stationary-point classification and finite-step convergence to an integral local maximizer without rounding. General tightness remains a shared claim; the new landscape guarantees introduce conditions involving non-integral λ>1.

C2.justification: V3 explains empirical loading tradeoffs and AdamW's weaker performance through landscape and implementation costs. V4 instead explains integral convergence through local attraction basins, strict-saddle escape, and the step-size denominator in Remark 4.2. Remark 4.11 adds the practical limitation that theoretical trigger constants are unknown, motivating adaptive thresholds.

D1.justification: V3 Sections 4.1–4.3 disclose graph preprocessing, Python/PyTorch implementation, CPU/RAM, optimizer settings, iteration budgets, and a code-access link; these disclosures are largely absent from v4. V4 identifies NetworkX for synthetic graph generation and describes adaptive threshold reduction, but supplies no numerical trigger threshold or reduction-factor setting.

R1.justification: V4 substantially expands positioning around saddle-escaping optimization, adding a dedicated Section 6 and comparisons with perturbation-based and constrained optimization approaches. It also adds Liu et al. (2025) and revises the EXPP discussion from v3's lack-of-tightness-analysis account to discussion of exactness guarantees under conservative penalty conditions.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contributions, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around theoretical questions. V3's two-method and benchmarking narrative becomes separate landscape and convergence sections with an explicit roadmap. Related work and appendices are reorganized, and references move before the appendices.

P2.justification: V4 adopts a two-column main-text layout, replaces the reformulation flowchart with a stationary-point set diagram, and removes the dataset table and six-network density/runtime grids. New three-panel convergence figures replace the earlier empirical displays, changing their metrics, captions, and visual organization.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially strengthens stationary-point and convergence analysis, but removes v3's broad empirical comparisons and code-access information. More decisively, its printed Algorithm 1 terminates at zero Frank–Wolfe gap, whereas Section 5.2 starts at a zero-gap saddle requiring escape. This unresolved conflict between the specified procedure and its central demonstration affects the finite-convergence claim, preventing a reliable net quality judgment despite the substantial theoretical gains.
